title: Transit Gateway, VPC Peering, RAM & VPC Lattice
summary: Connect many VPCs and accounts, share subnets, and wire up service-to-service traffic.
tldr: **VPC peering** is a direct, non-transitive link between two VPCs with no per-GB processing fee. Great for a few high-traffic pairs; a full mesh doesn't scale.

**Transit Gateway** is a Regional hub: VPCs, VPNs and DX attach once, routing is transitive, and route tables segment traffic. Share it across accounts with **AWS RAM**; connect Regions with **TGW peering**.
**VPC Lattice** connects *services*, not networks: HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC across VPCs and accounts with IAM auth policies, even with **overlapping CIDRs**, and no routes to manage.

keyFacts.text: Traffic can't pass through a peered VPC to a third VPC, VPN or internet gateway. CIDRs of peered VPCs must not overlap.
Transit Gateway charges per attachment-hour **and** per GB processed. Moving one heavy VPC pair to peering removes that processing fee.
**Inter-Region TGW peering** carries traffic on the AWS backbone, but you add static routes for the peer's CIDRs; routes don't propagate.
Out of IPs? Associate a **secondary IPv4 CIDR** with the VPC and create new subnets. You can't resize an existing VPC primary CIDR or subnet.
AWS reserves five IP addresses in every subnet, so a /28 gives 11 usable addresses. Plan subnets for awsvpc tasks that each take an IP.

traps: VPC peering isn't transitive; VPC A can't reach VPC C through VPC B.
Transit Gateway doesn't solve overlapping CIDRs; use PrivateLink or VPC Lattice.
You can't attach a VPC in another Region directly to a transit gateway; peer two transit gateways.
Changing a VPC's primary CIDR or editing a subnet's CIDR isn't possible; add a secondary CIDR.
A full mesh of peering connections across dozens of VPCs is the high-overhead answer.
